content: Brain fog is a term used to describe a sensation of mental cloudiness or an inability to think clearly, often likened to a physical obstruction in the brain. This term is frequently applied to describe neurocognitive symptoms experienced by individuals with conditions such as Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS) and fibromyalgia, among others. The underlying mechanisms of brain fog are not fully understood, but it is believed to be associated with factors such as increased cytokine activity, dysregulation of neurotransmitters, or psychological trauma. These mechanisms overlap with those implicated in certain mental health disorders, including depression and bipolar disorder. Although no specific studies have been conducted to identify the precise causes of brain fog, its similarity to symptoms of mental disorders suggests that it may involve frontal lobe hypometabolism or temporal lobe dysfunction, both of which are observed in unipolar depression. Brain fog is not formally recognized as a medical diagnosis, and there is no clinical evidence to confirm its existence as a distinct condition. Some clinicians propose that brain fog may represent a form of conversion disorder or somatization disorder. Given its overlap with symptoms of mental illnesses, it is possible that individuals reporting brain fog are experiencing underlying psychiatric conditions such as depression, schizophrenia, or bipolar disorder. For instance, the cognitive impairments associated with brain fog closely resemble the concentration difficulties seen in depression and the depressive phase of bipolar disorder, as well as the thought-blocking phenomena observed in schizophrenia. Brain fog can manifest as a symptom of various psychiatric and medical conditions, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, clinical depression, inattentive ADHD, and even as a side effect of chemotherapy. Additionally, individuals with Superior Canal Dehiscence Syndrome (SCDS) frequently report experiencing brain fog. The condition is characterized by persistent or episodic cognitive dysfunction, which may include forgetfulness, confusion, slowed thinking, distractibility, depersonalization, and difficulty finding the correct words when speaking or writing (dysphasia or aphasia). Many sufferers describe the sensation as feeling as though a cloud surrounds them, impairing their ability to process information or perceive things clearly. It is often likened to the experience of a hangover or zoning out. Brain fog may also contribute to feelings of detachment, discouragement, and depression. Diagnostic imaging techniques such as Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT), Positron Emission Tomography (PET), and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) can be employed to assess brain function in individuals experiencing brain fog. Neuropsychiatric testing may also be utilized to evaluate cognitive performance and identify potential underlying conditions. Treatment for brain fog varies depending on the underlying cause. Psychotherapy is sometimes recommended, although many individuals with ME/CFS report that psychotherapy can be unhelpful or even exhausting. Instead, they may prefer illness management strategies, such as taking a brief nap at the onset of brain fog symptoms. In cases where a more serious underlying pathology is identified, psychopharmacological interventions may be beneficial. Emerging evidence also suggests that neurofeedback may be an effective treatment option for managing brain fog.
